topics.name: HIV
topics.kicker: Retrovirus that attacks helper T cells · Can lead to AIDS without treatment
topics.briefing: HIV is a tiny virus with a sneaky strategy: it attacks helper T cells, the very immune cells that organize the body’s defenses. Scientists at France’s Pasteur Institute identified it in 1983, two years after doctors first reported the illness it can cause, AIDS. As of 2025, no vaccine had been approved, but since 1996, combinations of medicines have let people living with HIV keep the virus in check and live long, healthy lives.
topics.answerHtml: HIV (accept human immunodeficiency virus; accept HIV-1 or HIV-2; prompt on AIDS or acquired immunodeficiency syndrome by asking for the virus; do not accept “SIV” or “HPV”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Luc Montagnier and Françoise Barré-Sinoussi [“bah-RAY see-noo-SEE”] shared the 2008 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for identifying this agent at the Pasteur Institute in Paris. Their team reported it in 1983, two years after American doctors first described the illness it causes.
tossups.r: This virus copies its RNA into DNA using reverse transcriptase. For 10 points, name this virus that attacks helper T cells and causes AIDS.

tossups.p: In 1970, Howard Temin and David Baltimore separately discovered the type of enzyme this agent uses to copy its genes from RNA into DNA, years before this agent itself was known. That error-prone enzyme helps this agent mutate quickly, one reason that, as of 2025, no vaccine against it had been approved.
tossups.r: That enzyme, reverse transcriptase, is blocked by the drug AZT. For 10 points, name this retrovirus that attacks helper T cells and causes AIDS.

tossups.p: Timothy Ray Brown, nicknamed the “Berlin patient,” became the first person known to be cured of this infection after stem cell transplants given to treat his leukemia. His donor carried two copies of a mutation called delta 32 in the gene for CCR5, a coreceptor that most strains of this virus use to enter cells.
tossups.r: This virus’s surface protein gp120 attaches to the CD4 receptor. For 10 points, name this virus that destroys helper T cells and can lead to AIDS.

tossups.p: This virus’s cone-shaped capsid is built from a protein called p24 and holds two copies of its RNA genome. Spikes on this virus’s outer envelope are made of the proteins gp120 and gp41, which grab a receptor called CD4 and help the virus fuse with a cell.
tossups.r: Researchers at the Pasteur Institute identified it in 1983. For 10 points, name this retrovirus that infects helper T cells and causes AIDS.

tossups.p: Cleve Jones started a giant memorial quilt in San Francisco to honor people who had died of the illness this virus causes, and in October 1987 its panels were first laid out on the National Mall in Washington.
tossups.r: Every December 1, World AIDS Day raises awareness of this virus, whose symbol is a looped red ribbon. For 10 points, name this virus that weakens the immune system.

tossups.p: Jerome Horwitz first made the drug AZT, or zidovudine, in 1964 as a possible cancer treatment, but in 1987 it became the first approved medicine against this virus. AZT works by jamming the enzyme this virus uses to turn its RNA into DNA.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this virus that weakens the immune system by destroying helper T cells.

tossups.p: Scientist David Ho was named _Time_ magazine’s 1996 Man of the Year for helping develop combination therapy against this virus. That “cocktail” approach, which mixes protease inhibitors with other medicines, let many people living with this virus keep it under control for decades.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this virus that is treated with antiretroviral drugs and can cause AIDS.

tossups.p: In 1985, Indiana teenager Ryan White was barred from his middle school after his diagnosis, and he fought in court to return to class. A 1990 law named for him, the Ryan White CARE Act, has helped pay for medical care for people living with this virus.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this virus that attacks helper T cells and can lead to AIDS.

tossups.p: In 2003, President George W. Bush announced PEPFAR, an emergency relief plan that went on to pay for treatment for millions of people with this virus, especially in Africa. In 1991, basketball star Magic Johnson announced that he had this virus and retired from the Los Angeles Lakers.
tossups.r: This virus uses reverse transcriptase to copy its RNA into DNA. For 10 points, name this virus that attacks helper T cells and can cause AIDS.

tossups.p: Genetic studies suggest that this virus crossed into humans from chimpanzees in central Africa in the early 1900s, and that its main strain began spreading from the city of Kinshasa. It belongs to the lentiviruses, or “slow viruses,” which can take years to cause symptoms.
tossups.r: This virus infects and destroys helper T cells. For 10 points, name this virus that causes AIDS.

tossups.p: On June 5, 1981, a report from the Centers for Disease Control described five previously healthy young men in Los Angeles with a rare kind of pneumonia. That report was the first official account of the illness caused by this virus.
tossups.r: That illness was soon named AIDS. For 10 points, name this virus that weakens the body’s immune system by attacking helper T cells.

tossups.p: Drugs called integrase inhibitors stop this virus from splicing a DNA copy of its genes into a host cell’s chromosomes. A person with this virus is diagnosed with the syndrome it causes if the number of CD4 cells in a cubic millimeter of blood falls below 200.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this virus that destroys helper T cells, which is kept in check with antiretroviral therapy.

tossups.p: American scientist Robert Gallo announced in 1984 that he had found the cause of a new illness, a virus he called HTLV-III, setting off a long dispute with French researchers over credit.
tossups.r: This virus’s surface protein gp120 locks onto the CD4 receptor of the cells it attacks. For 10 points, name this virus that causes AIDS.

tossups.p: The musical _Rent_ and Tony Kushner’s play _Angels in America_ both include characters living with the illness this virus causes. In 1991, basketball star Magic Johnson announced that he had tested positive for this virus, and he retired from the Los Angeles Lakers.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this virus that is kept in check with antiretroviral therapy.

tossups.p: This member of the lentiviruses can hide inside the DNA of resting cells for years, one reason it is so hard to cure. Its copying enzyme makes so many mistakes that it mutates quickly, which helps it resist any single drug used against it.
tossups.r: That enzyme is reverse transcriptase. The illness this virus causes was first reported in 1981. For 10 points, name this virus that attacks helper T cells and causes AIDS.

clues.t: Causes AIDS (acquired immunodeficiency syndrome) if it is not treated
Attacks helper T cells, the white blood cells that organize the body’s immune defenses
Weakens the immune system, so the body has trouble fighting off other infections
Kept in check (but not cured) by antiretroviral therapy, a combination of medicines
Its awareness symbol is the red ribbon; World AIDS Day is held every December 1
A retrovirus: its genes are stored as RNA, which it copies into DNA inside the cells it infects
Uses the enzyme reverse transcriptase to copy its RNA into DNA
Its surface protein gp120 latches onto the CD4 receptor on helper T cells
Identified in 1983 by Luc Montagnier and Françoise Barré-Sinoussi at the Pasteur Institute in Paris
The illness it causes was first officially reported on June 5, 1981, when the CDC described five young men in Los Angeles with a rare pneumonia
AZT (zidovudine), first made in 1964 as a possible cancer drug, became the first approved medicine against it in 1987
Drug “cocktails” used from 1996 kept it under control; David Ho was _Time_’s 1996 Man of the Year for this work
Crossed into humans from chimpanzees in central Africa in the early 1900s; a related chimpanzee virus is called SIV
Indiana teen Ryan White fought to return to school after his diagnosis; the 1990 Ryan White CARE Act is named for him
Montagnier and Barré-Sinoussi shared the 2008 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for discovering it
American Robert Gallo reported it in 1984 under the name HTLV-III, starting a long dispute over credit
Howard Temin and David Baltimore discovered reverse transcriptase in 1970 and shared a 1975 Nobel Prize
Its cone-shaped capsid of the protein p24 holds two copies of its RNA; envelope spikes of gp120 and gp41 help it enter cells
Also uses a coreceptor called CCR5; people with two copies of the CCR5 delta 32 mutation resist the most common strains
Timothy Ray Brown, the “Berlin patient,” was the first person known to be cured, after stem cell transplants from a donor with that mutation
Its enzyme integrase splices its DNA copy into the host cell’s chromosomes; integrase inhibitors and protease inhibitors block its enzymes
A lentivirus (“slow virus”) that can hide inside the DNA of resting cells for years, which makes it hard to cure
Its error-prone copying makes it mutate fast, so it resists single drugs; as of 2025, no vaccine against it had been approved
AIDS is diagnosed when CD4 cells fall below 200 per cubic millimeter of blood, or when opportunistic infections appear
PEPFAR, an emergency relief plan announced by President George W. Bush in 2003, paid for treatment for millions of people abroad
In 1991, Lakers star Magic Johnson announced he had tested positive for it and retired from the Lakers
Cleve Jones began the AIDS Memorial Quilt in San Francisco; its panels were first laid out on the National Mall in October 1987
The musical _Rent_ and Tony Kushner’s play _Angels in America_ include characters living with AIDS

trap.title: Virus or syndrome?
trap.body: HIV is the virus; AIDS (acquired immunodeficiency syndrome) is the late stage of illness it can cause when it is not treated. Answer lines that want the virus may only prompt on AIDS, and a question that asks for the syndrome may not accept the virus. Other three-letter viruses, like HPV (human papillomavirus) and SIV (the related virus in chimpanzees and monkeys), are wrong.
trap.fix: Listen for the noun at the end. “This virus” or “this retrovirus” means HIV; “this syndrome” or “this condition” means AIDS. If you get a prompt after saying AIDS, answer “HIV” or “human immunodeficiency virus.”
trap.line: Real answer line: HIV (accept human immunodeficiency virus; prompt on AIDS or acquired immunodeficiency syndrome)

topics.name: Bacteria
topics.kicker: Single-celled prokaryotes · A few cause disease; most are harmless or helpful
topics.dates: First described by Leeuwenhoek in the 1670s
topics.briefing: Bacteria are single-celled living things, nearly all far too small to see without a microscope, yet they live almost everywhere: in soil, in boiling hot springs, and by the trillions in your own gut. Antonie van Leeuwenhoek first spotted them through his homemade microscopes in the 1670s and called them “animalcules.” A few cause illnesses like strep throat, but most are harmless or helpful, from the ones that turn milk into yogurt to the ones that help bean plants get nitrogen.
topics.answerHtml: Bacteria (accept bacterium or eubacteria; prompt on prokaryotes, microbes, or germs; do not accept “archaea” or “viruses”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Carl Woese compared ribosomal RNA from many microbes in 1977 and concluded that the archaea, long lumped together with this group, form a very different branch of life. Unlike archaea, most members of this domain build their cell walls out of peptidoglycan [“pep-tih-doh-GLY-kan”].
tossups.r: Members of this domain reproduce by binary fission. For 10 points, name these single-celled prokaryotes, some of which cause strep throat and tuberculosis.

tossups.p: In the 1960s, Thomas Brock found a heat-loving species of these organisms in a Yellowstone hot spring, and its heat-resistant enzyme, Taq polymerase, later made it much easier to copy DNA using PCR. That species is named Thermus aquaticus [“THER-mus uh-KWAT-ih-kus”].
tossups.r: These organisms have no nucleus and usually keep their DNA in one circular chromosome. For 10 points, name these prokaryotes that can be killed by antibiotics.

tossups.p: Jennifer Doudna and Emmanuelle Charpentier won the 2020 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for turning CRISPR, a defense system these organisms use against invading viruses, into a tool for editing genes. The viruses that infect these organisms are called phages.
tossups.r: Antibiotics such as penicillin kill these organisms but do not work on viruses. For 10 points, name these single-celled prokaryotes.

tossups.p: Frederick Griffith showed in 1928 that a harmless “rough” strain of one species of these organisms could turn deadly to mice after being mixed with a heat-killed “smooth” strain, a change called transformation. These organisms can also share small rings of DNA called plasmids.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these prokaryotes that reproduce by splitting in two, a process called binary fission.

tossups.p: In a 1683 letter, Antonie van Leeuwenhoek [“LAY-vun-hook”] described these organisms in plaque scraped from his own teeth, calling them tiny “animalcules.” Robert Koch later proved that specific types of these organisms cause the diseases anthrax and tuberculosis.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these microbes, some of which cause illnesses that can be treated with antibiotics.

tossups.p: The Hawaiian bobtail squid hides its shadow using light made by Vibrio fischeri [“VIB-ree-oh FISH-er-eye”], a species of these organisms that glows only when enough of its members gather, a process called quorum sensing.
tossups.r: Many of these organisms swim using whip-like flagella. For 10 points, name these prokaryotes, whose shapes include round cocci and rod-shaped bacilli.

tossups.p: MRSA is a strain of Staphylococcus aureus, one of these organisms, that resists the antibiotic methicillin. In 1928, Alexander Fleming noticed that a mold growing in a petri dish had killed the colonies of these organisms around it.
tossups.r: That mold made penicillin. For 10 points, name these single-celled microbes that are killed by antibiotics.

tossups.p: Clostridium and Bacillus are types of these organisms that can survive boiling, drying, and harsh chemicals by forming tough, dormant endospores. In 1876, Robert Koch showed that one rod-shaped species of these organisms causes the disease anthrax.
tossups.r: Like all members of their domain, these organisms have no nucleus. For 10 points, name these single-celled prokaryotes, which reproduce by binary fission.

tossups.p: Fanny Hesse suggested that her husband, who worked with Robert Koch, grow these organisms on agar, a jelly made from seaweed. In 1887, Koch’s assistant Julius Petri invented a shallow covered dish for growing them.
tossups.r: Koch’s postulates are rules for proving that one of these organisms causes a disease. For 10 points, name these germs, some of which cause strep throat.

tossups.p: Rocky mounds called stromatolites [“stroh-MAT-uh-lyts”] were built in shallow seas by a group of these organisms that was once misnamed blue-green algae. That group’s photosynthesis began filling Earth’s air with oxygen about 2.4 billion years ago, in the Great Oxidation Event.
tossups.r: Like all members of their domain, they lack a nucleus. For 10 points, name these prokaryotes, which include E. coli.

tossups.p: The antibiotic streptomycin attacks the small 70S ribosomes of these organisms, which differ from the larger 80S ribosomes in human cells. Penicillin works by stopping these organisms from building cell walls out of peptidoglycan.
tossups.r: These organisms can be sorted into two groups by Gram staining. For 10 points, name these single-celled prokaryotes, some of which cause strep throat and cholera.

tossups.p: During conjugation, one of these organisms can pass a copy of a plasmid to a neighbor through a tube called a pilus. Viruses called phages can also carry genes from one of these organisms to another, in a process called transduction.
tossups.r: These organisms reproduce by binary fission. For 10 points, name these prokaryotes, some of which have become resistant to antibiotics.

tossups.p: According to the endosymbiotic theory, mitochondria began as one of these organisms that was swallowed by a larger cell. Rhizobium [“ry-ZOH-bee-um”], a type of these organisms that lives in nodules on the roots of beans and peas, turns nitrogen from the air into a form plants can use.
tossups.r: Along with fungi, these organisms are important decomposers. For 10 points, name these microbes that include E. coli.

tossups.p: Yersinia pestis [“yer-SIN-ee-uh PES-tis”], a species of these organisms, caused the Black Death in the 1300s. Another species, E. coli, lives in the human large intestine, where gut members of this group help make vitamin K.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these single-celled organisms that lack a nucleus, some of which cause diseases treated with antibiotics.

tossups.p: In a test developed by Hans Christian Gram in 1884, these organisms are stained with purple crystal violet and then a pink dye called safranin. Types with thick peptidoglycan walls stay purple, while types with a thin wall and an outer membrane turn pink.
tossups.r: Their three main shapes are cocci, bacilli, and spirilla. For 10 points, name these single-celled prokaryotes.

clues.t: Single-celled prokaryotes: they have no nucleus and no membrane-bound organelles
Three main shapes: round cocci, rod-shaped bacilli, and spiral spirilla
Killed by antibiotics such as penicillin, which do not work on viruses
Some cause diseases such as strep throat, tuberculosis, and cholera
Reproduce by splitting in two, a process called binary fission
Their cell walls are built from peptidoglycan; penicillin stops them from building those walls
Gram staining (Hans Christian Gram, 1884) sorts them into purple Gram-positive and pink Gram-negative types
First seen by Antonie van Leeuwenhoek, who called them “animalcules”; in 1683 he found them in plaque from his teeth
Usually keep one circular chromosome in a region called the nucleoid, plus small DNA rings called plasmids
Robert Koch linked specific ones to anthrax (1876) and tuberculosis (1882); Koch’s postulates test whether a microbe causes a disease
Alexander Fleming discovered penicillin in 1928 when a mold killed the colonies growing in his petri dish
Rhizobium in root nodules of beans and peas turns nitrogen from the air into a form plants can use
E. coli lives in the human large intestine, where gut species help make vitamin K
Important decomposers along with fungi; many swim with whip-like flagella and grip surfaces with hair-like pili
Carl Woese compared ribosomal RNA in 1977 and split prokaryotes into two groups, later called domains: these and the archaea
Their small 70S ribosomes differ from the 80S ribosomes in human cells, so streptomycin can attack them
Clostridium and Bacillus survive boiling and drying as tough, dormant endospores
Frederick Griffith’s 1928 experiment with “rough” and “smooth” strains in mice revealed transformation
Share plasmids through a pilus in conjugation; viruses called phages carry genes between them in transduction
CRISPR began as their defense against viruses; Jennifer Doudna and Emmanuelle Charpentier won the 2020 Chemistry Nobel for making it a gene-editing tool
Taq polymerase, used to copy DNA in PCR, comes from Thermus aquaticus, found by Thomas Brock in a Yellowstone hot spring
MRSA is a strain of Staphylococcus aureus that resists the antibiotic methicillin
Quorum sensing: chemical signals let them sense their own numbers, as when Vibrio fischeri glow inside the Hawaiian bobtail squid
Grown on agar (suggested by Fanny Hesse) in shallow dishes invented in 1887 by Koch’s assistant Julius Petri
A photosynthetic group once called blue-green algae built stromatolites and filled the air with oxygen starting about 2.4 billion years ago
Endosymbiotic theory: mitochondria and chloroplasts began as ancient ones swallowed by a larger cell
Yersinia pestis, one species, caused the Black Death in the 1300s

trap.title: Bacteria, archaea, or viruses?
trap.body: Bacteria and archaea are both single-celled prokaryotes with no nucleus, and until Carl Woese’s work in 1977 they were lumped together. Viruses are not cells at all and are not killed by antibiotics. Saying “prokaryotes,” “microbes,” or “germs” is too general and earns only a prompt.
trap.fix: Peptidoglycan walls, Gram staining, antibiotics, penicillin, E. coli, and diseases like strep throat mean bacteria. Methane-making, walls with no peptidoglycan, and “the third domain” mean archaea; both groups include heat lovers, so a hot spring alone does not decide it. A protein capsid and needing a host cell to copy itself mean viruses.
trap.line: Real answer line: Bacteria (accept bacterium; prompt on prokaryotes or microbes; do not accept “archaea” or “viruses”)

topics.name: Blood types
topics.kicker: Categories like A, B, AB, and O · Must match for a safe transfusion
topics.briefing: Every person’s red blood cells carry tiny markers called antigens that sort blood into types like A, B, AB, and O, each either Rh-positive or Rh-negative. Karl Landsteiner discovered the first three types in 1901 and explained why some early transfusions saved lives while others failed: mismatched blood clumps together. That is why type O-negative donors, whose red cells lack the A, B, and Rh antigens, are called “universal donors.”
topics.answerHtml: Blood types (accept blood groups or the ABO system; prompt on blood or Rh factor; do not accept “red blood cells” or “antigens”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Karl Landsteiner noticed in 1901 that red cells from some people clumped when mixed with serum from others, so he sorted human blood into three groups. His third group, which he first called C, was later renamed.
tossups.r: That group became type O, whose negative form belongs to universal donors. For 10 points, name these categories of blood, which also include A, B, and AB.

tossups.p: In 1902, Alfred von Decastello and Adriano Sturli, two colleagues of Karl Landsteiner, found a rare fourth group whose red cells carry two different antigens at once. Their discovery completed the system Landsteiner had begun the year before.
tossups.r: People in that group who are also Rh-positive are universal recipients. For 10 points, name these categories of blood, such as A, B, AB, and O.

tossups.p: Czech doctor Jan Janský [“YAHN-skee”] sorted human blood into four groups in 1907, numbering them with Roman numerals from I to IV. Karl Landsteiner had described three of those groups six years earlier.
tossups.r: Mismatched categories make red cells clump during a transfusion. For 10 points, name these categories of blood, such as A, B, AB, and O.

tossups.p: World Blood Donor Day is held every June 14, the birthday of the scientist who discovered these categories. That scientist, Karl Landsteiner, won the 1930 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for the discovery.
tossups.r: Donors and patients must be matched, or red cells clump in a reaction called agglutination. For 10 points, name these categories of blood, such as A-positive and O-negative.

tossups.p: People with the rare Bombay phenotype, first described in 1952 in the Indian city of Mumbai, then called Bombay, lack a sugar marker called the H antigen, so they can safely receive blood only from other people with the same rare trait.
tossups.r: Their blood can be mistaken for type O. For 10 points, name these categories of blood, which are set by antigens on red blood cells.

tossups.p: Shots of a medicine called RhoGAM keep a mother who lacks a certain factor from making antibodies that could harm a later baby who has it. In 1940, Karl Landsteiner and Alexander Wiener described that factor, named for the rhesus monkeys used in their research.
tossups.r: That factor makes these categories positive or negative. For 10 points, name these categories of blood, such as A-positive and O-negative.

tossups.p: The gene behind these categories, found on chromosome 9, makes an enzyme that adds one of two particular sugars to the surface of red blood cells. One version of that gene makes a broken enzyme that adds neither sugar.
tossups.r: That version is the recessive O allele. For 10 points, name these inherited categories of blood, which also include A, B, and AB.

tossups.p: Systems for sorting these classifications include Kell, Kidd, and Duffy, as well as the MN system found by Karl Landsteiner and Philip Levine in 1927. Lacking the Duffy antigen, a trait common in parts of Africa, helps protect people against one kind of malaria.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these classifications of blood, the best known of which include A, B, AB, and O.

tossups.p: In Japan, many people believe these categories predict a person’s personality, though scientists have found no good evidence for it. Mixing samples from two mismatched categories makes red cells clump together, a reaction called agglutination [“uh-gloo-tih-NAY-shun”].
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these categories of blood, such as A, B, AB, and O, which are checked before a transfusion.

tossups.p: In 1907, Reuben Ottenberg performed the first transfusion in which the donor’s and patient’s blood were tested and cross-matched beforehand. Many earlier transfusions had failed because no one checked whether the blood matched. Hospitals cross-match blood because the patient’s antibodies can destroy mismatched red cells.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these categories of blood, including O-negative, whose donors are called universal donors.

tossups.p: A person’s plasma carries antibodies against whichever of the two main red-cell antigens that person lacks, so someone whose red cells have neither antigen makes both kinds of antibody. These antibodies form early in life, even without a transfusion.
tossups.r: That person has type O, while a person with both antigens has type AB. For 10 points, name these categories of blood that must be matched for a transfusion.

tossups.p: Hemolytic [“hee-moh-LIT-ik”] disease of the newborn can occur when a mother’s antibodies attack her baby’s red cells because of a mismatch in the Rh system. Red cells that carry the most important Rh antigen, called D, are labeled positive.
tossups.r: Red cells without it are labeled negative. For 10 points, name these categories of blood, such as AB-positive and O-negative.

tossups.p: The scientist who discovered these categories also showed, with Erwin Popper, that a virus causes polio. That Austrian scientist later moved to New York to work at the Rockefeller Institute.
tossups.r: That scientist was Karl Landsteiner. For 10 points, name these categories of blood, such as A, B, AB, and O.

tossups.p: Biology classes use these categories as a classic example of codominance, since a person who inherits two different dominant alleles shows both of their antigens. These categories are also an example of multiple alleles, since one gene has three common versions.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these inherited categories of blood, such as A, B, AB, and O.

tossups.p: Sugar chains attached to proteins and fats in red blood cell membranes act as the antigens that set these categories, and the two main antigens differ by just one sugar at the end of the chain. Two parents with different categories can have a child whose category matches neither parent’s.
tossups.r: A quick test checks these categories by mixing blood with anti-A and anti-B serums. For 10 points, name these categories of blood, such as A, B, AB, and O.

clues.t: The four main ones are A, B, AB, and O
Each is also positive or negative, depending on whether the red cells carry the Rh factor
Must be matched before a transfusion, or the patient’s antibodies attack the donor’s red cells
Type O-negative donors are “universal donors”; type AB-positive patients are “universal recipients”
Set by antigens, marker molecules on the surface of red blood cells
Karl Landsteiner discovered the first three groups in 1901; his group “C” was later renamed O
The Rh factor is named for rhesus monkeys; Landsteiner and Alexander Wiener described it in 1940
Plasma carries antibodies against the antigens a person lacks: type A blood has anti-B antibodies, and type O has both
Mismatched blood clumps together, a reaction called agglutination
The A and B alleles are codominant, so a person who inherits both has type AB
The O allele is recessive; with three common alleles, the system is a classic case of multiple alleles
Parents with types A and B can have a child of any of the four types if each carries a hidden O allele
A quick test mixes drops of blood with anti-A and anti-B serums and checks which drops clump
Landsteiner won the 1930 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine; with Erwin Popper he also showed that a virus causes polio
Alfred von Decastello and Adriano Sturli found the rare fourth group, AB, in 1902
Czech doctor Jan Janský sorted blood into four groups numbered I to IV in 1907
Reuben Ottenberg performed the first transfusion with tested, cross-matched blood in 1907
World Blood Donor Day is June 14, Landsteiner’s birthday
Their gene, on chromosome 9, makes an enzyme that adds sugars to red cells; the O version makes a broken enzyme
The A and B antigens are sugar chains on red cell membranes, built on top of a base marker called the H antigen
The rare Bombay phenotype (described 1952) lacks the H antigen, looks like type O, and can receive only Bombay blood
Rh mismatch can cause hemolytic disease of the newborn; RhoGAM shots keep an Rh-negative mother from making the harmful antibodies
Rh-positive red cells carry the D antigen, the most important Rh antigen
Other systems include MN (Landsteiner and Philip Levine, 1927), Kell, Kidd, and Duffy; lacking the Duffy antigen helps protect against one kind of malaria
In Japan, a popular belief with no good scientific support links them to personality

trap.title: Types, cells, or factor?
trap.body: Tossups on this topic are full of red blood cells, antigens, antibodies, plasma, and the Rh factor, and several of those are their own answer lines on this site (Blood, Red blood cells, Antibodies). Buzzing with one of those parts is wrong. “Rh factor” names only one piece of the system and “blood” is too general, so each earns just a prompt.
trap.fix: If the question asks for “these categories,” “these classifications,” or “these groups,” and the giveaway lists A, B, AB, and O, say “blood types.” If it asks for “this factor” named for monkeys, say “Rh factor.” If it asks for “these proteins in plasma,” say “antibodies.”
trap.line: Real answer line: Blood types (accept blood groups or ABO system; prompt on Rh factor; do not accept “red blood cells”)

topics.name: Chlorophyll
topics.kicker: Green pigment that captures light · Has a magnesium ion at its center
topics.briefing: Chlorophyll is the green pigment that lets plants feed on sunlight. It soaks up mostly red and blue light and bounces green light back, which is why leaves look green, and each molecule holds a single magnesium ion at the center of a ring. In autumn, many trees break their chlorophyll down, uncovering the yellow and orange pigments that were hiding in the leaves all summer.
topics.answerHtml: Chlorophyll (accept chlorophyll a or chlorophyll b; prompt on pigment; do not accept “chloroplasts” or “carotenoids”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: French chemists Pierre Joseph Pelletier and Joseph Bienaimé Caventou isolated this substance in 1817, a few years before the same pair isolated quinine. They gave it a name built from Greek words for “pale green” and “leaf.”
tossups.r: This pigment absorbs mostly red and blue light. For 10 points, name this green pigment found in chloroplasts.

tossups.p: Richard Willstätter [“VIL-shtet-er”] won the 1915 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for studying this compound and other plant pigments. Each molecule of this compound holds a magnesium ion at the center of a flat ring.
tossups.r: This compound reflects green light. For 10 points, name this pigment that captures light energy for photosynthesis.

tossups.p: In 1960, Robert Burns Woodward’s team built this complicated molecule from scratch in the lab, part of the work that earned Woodward a Nobel Prize five years later. Its structure includes a long tail made from a molecule called phytol [“FY-tawl”].
tossups.r: This molecule reflects green light. For 10 points, name this pigment that plants use for photosynthesis.

tossups.p: A long hydrocarbon tail made from phytol anchors this molecule in the thylakoid membrane. Its head is a flat ring with a magnesium ion at the center, much like the iron-holding heme group in hemoglobin.
tossups.r: Paper chromatography of spinach extract separates this pigment from orange carotene. For 10 points, name this green pigment that absorbs light inside chloroplasts.

tossups.p: One form of this molecule has a methyl group at a spot where a second form has an aldehyde group, so the two forms absorb slightly different colors. That second form is called an accessory pigment because it passes the energy it absorbs to the first form.
tossups.r: Both forms hold a magnesium ion at the center of a ring. For 10 points, name this green pigment that captures sunlight for photosynthesis.

tossups.p: A form of this pigment labeled f, discovered in 2010 in stromatolites from Australia’s Shark Bay, can absorb far-red light. Cyanobacteria, algae, and plants all use the form of this pigment labeled a.
tossups.r: This pigment reflects green light. For 10 points, name this pigment found in the chloroplasts of plant cells.

tossups.p: Brown algae such as kelp use a form of this pigment labeled c, along with an orange-brown pigment called fucoxanthin [“fyoo-koh-ZAN-thin”] that hides its usual color. Like plants, kelp also use the form of this pigment labeled a.
tossups.r: In land plants, this pigment comes in forms a and b. For 10 points, name this green pigment that captures light for photosynthesis.

tossups.p: Botanist Mikhail Tsvet [“TSVET”] invented chromatography in the early 1900s by washing leaf extracts through a column of chalk powder, separating this pigment from others. In a classroom version, spinach extract on paper splits into this pigment, yellow xanthophylls, and orange carotene.
tossups.r: This pigment absorbs red and blue light but reflects green. For 10 points, name this green pigment found in chloroplasts.

tossups.p: A solution of this pigment glows red under ultraviolet light, a property called fluorescence. In living leaves, electrons that light knocks loose from this pigment are replaced by electrons taken from water, which releases oxygen.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this green pigment that absorbs light in the thylakoids of chloroplasts.

tossups.p: Seedlings grown in darkness turn pale yellow, a condition called etiolation [“ee-tee-oh-LAY-shun”], because most flowering plants need light to finish making this pigment. A shortage of iron, magnesium, or nitrogen can also yellow leaves by lowering this pigment, a condition called chlorosis.
tossups.r: Plants look green because this pigment reflects green light. For 10 points, name this pigment that captures sunlight for photosynthesis.

tossups.p: Theodor Engelmann spread a prism’s rainbow across a strand of algae and found that oxygen-loving bacteria crowded around the red and blue zones, matching the colors this pigment absorbs best. That experiment produced the first action spectrum.
tossups.r: Because this pigment reflects green light, most leaves look green. For 10 points, name this pigment found in chloroplasts.

tossups.p: Special pairs of this molecule called P680 and P700 sit at the reaction centers of the two photosystems. Light-harvesting antenna complexes, packed with hundreds of molecules of this pigment, pass captured energy along to those centers.
tossups.r: This pigment sits in the thylakoid membranes of chloroplasts. For 10 points, name this green pigment that absorbs light energy for photosynthesis.

tossups.p: Hans Fischer won the 1930 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for work on the structures of heme and this molecule, which are built around similar rings. Instead of heme’s iron, this molecule holds a magnesium ion.
tossups.r: This pigment absorbs mostly red and blue light. For 10 points, name this green pigment that plants use to capture light.

tossups.p: The absorption spectrum of this pigment shows two tall peaks, one in the blue-violet range and one in the red, with a deep dip in the green. Each fall, many trees break this pigment down, letting yellow and orange carotenoids show through.
tossups.r: This pigment is packed into chloroplasts. For 10 points, name this green pigment found in the leaves of plants.

tossups.p: Four nitrogen atoms in this molecule’s porphyrin [“POR-fuh-rin”] ring hold a central magnesium ion. This molecule’s name comes from Greek words meaning “pale green” and “leaf,” and Robert Burns Woodward first built it in the lab in 1960.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this pigment that absorbs red and blue light inside chloroplasts and gives plants their green color.

clues.t: The green pigment that captures light for photosynthesis
Found inside chloroplasts, packed into the thylakoid membranes
Absorbs mostly red and blue light and reflects green, which is why leaves look green
Found in plants, algae, and cyanobacteria, but not in animals or fungi
Holds a magnesium ion at the center of a flat ring called a porphyrin
Its ring looks much like heme in hemoglobin, which holds iron instead of magnesium
Plants have two main forms: a, the main one, and b, an accessory pigment that passes energy to a
Its name comes from Greek words for “pale green” and “leaf”
Many trees break it down in autumn, letting yellow and orange carotenoids show in fall leaves
When light knocks an electron loose from it, splitting water replaces that electron and releases oxygen
Paper chromatography of spinach extract separates it from yellow xanthophylls and orange carotene
Leaves that lack it turn yellow, a condition called chlorosis, often from too little iron, magnesium, or nitrogen
Isolated and named in 1817 by French chemists Pierre Joseph Pelletier and Joseph Bienaimé Caventou, who later isolated quinine
Richard Willstätter won the 1915 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for studying it and other plant pigments
Hans Fischer won the 1930 Chemistry Nobel for work on the structures of heme and this molecule
Robert Burns Woodward’s team first built it from scratch in the lab in 1960
A long hydrocarbon tail made from phytol anchors it in the thylakoid membrane
Form a has a methyl group where form b has an aldehyde group
Special pairs called P680 and P700 sit at the reaction centers of photosystems II and I; antenna complexes funnel energy to them
A solution of it glows red under ultraviolet light, a property called fluorescence
Mikhail Tsvet invented chromatography in the early 1900s by separating it and other leaf pigments on a column of chalk
A form labeled f, found in 2010 in stromatolites from Australia’s Shark Bay, absorbs far-red light
Brown algae such as kelp use form c plus an orange-brown pigment called fucoxanthin
Seedlings grown in the dark turn pale yellow (etiolation) because most flowering plants need light to finish making it
Theodor Engelmann used a prism, algae, and oxygen-loving bacteria to show that red and blue light work best
Its absorption spectrum has two peaks, in the blue-violet and the red, with a dip in the green

trap.title: Pigment or organelle?
trap.body: Chlorophyll is the green pigment molecule; chloroplasts are the organelles that hold it, and thylakoids are the membranes inside them where it sits. The names look almost alike, so a fast buzz can come out wrong. Yellow and orange carotenoids and red anthocyanins are other plant pigments, and they are wrong too.
trap.fix: Listen for the noun. “This pigment” or “this molecule,” especially with a magnesium ion at its center, means chlorophyll. “This organelle” with its own DNA means chloroplast. “These orange pigments” such as carotene mean carotenoids.
trap.line: Real answer line: Chlorophyll (accept chlorophyll a or chlorophyll b; prompt on pigment; do not accept “chloroplast”)

topics.name: Chordates
topics.kicker: Animal phylum with a notochord · Includes all vertebrates, even humans
topics.dates: Fossils date back more than 500 million years
topics.briefing: Chordates are the animal phylum you belong to. At some point in life, every chordate has a flexible rod called a notochord, a hollow nerve cord along its back, slits in its throat, and a tail that extends past the anus, even if, like humans, it has some of them only as an embryo. Besides all the vertebrates, the phylum includes odd ocean cousins: tube-shaped sea squirts and little fishlike lancelets.
topics.answerHtml: Chordates (accept Chordata; prompt on deuterostomes; do not accept “vertebrates” or “hemichordates”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Charles Walcott described Pikaia, a small, ribbon-shaped animal from the Burgess Shale, in 1911, and it was long considered one of the earliest known members of this phylum. Its fossils show segmented muscle blocks called myomeres [“MY-oh-meerz”].
tossups.r: Members of this phylum have a notochord at some point in their lives. For 10 points, name this phylum that includes all vertebrates.

tossups.p: In 1928, Walter Garstang suggested that vertebrates evolved from tadpole-like sea squirt larvae that never changed into the adult form. Tunicates, the group that includes sea squirts, are thought to be the closest invertebrate relatives of vertebrates.
tossups.r: Members of this phylum have pharyngeal slits and a post-anal tail at some stage. For 10 points, name this phylum that includes fish, birds, and humans.

tossups.p: Tunicates in this phylum are the only animals known to make cellulose, which stiffens their tough outer covering, or tunic. Some tunicates, called salps, are barrel-shaped and swim by jet propulsion, pumping water through their bodies.
tossups.r: This phylum also includes lancelets and all vertebrates. For 10 points, name this phylum defined by a notochord and a dorsal hollow nerve cord.

tossups.p: A groove called the endostyle [“EN-doh-style”], which helps tunicates and lancelets trap food, is thought to match the thyroid gland of other members of this phylum. Larval lampreys, called ammocoetes [“AM-oh-seets”], also have an endostyle.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this phylum whose members have a notochord at some stage, including all vertebrates.

tossups.p: V-shaped muscle blocks called myomeres flex the bodies of lancelets, small fishlike filter feeders in this phylum that burrow in sand. Lancelets, also called amphioxus [“am-fee-OK-sus”], keep all of this phylum’s hallmark traits as adults.
tossups.r: Those traits include a notochord and pharyngeal slits. For 10 points, name this animal phylum that includes all vertebrates.

tossups.p: Larvaceans [“lar-VAY-shunz”] are tiny tunicates in this phylum that keep their tadpole shape for life and build see-through mucus “houses” to filter food from seawater. Other tunicates, such as sea squirts, lose most of this phylum’s hallmark traits as adults.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this phylum defined by a notochord, a dorsal hollow nerve cord, pharyngeal slits, and a post-anal tail.

tossups.p: Acorn worms have pharyngeal slits but are placed in a separate phylum, next to the echinoderms. Like echinoderms, members of this phylum are deuterostomes [“DOO-tuh-roh-stohmz”], meaning an embryo’s first opening becomes the anus.
tossups.r: This phylum also includes lancelets and tunicates. For 10 points, name this phylum of animals with a notochord, which includes fish, frogs, and humans.

tossups.p: Haikouichthys [“hy-koo-IK-thiss”], found among China’s Chengjiang fossils, is one of the earliest known fishlike members of this phylum, from more than 500 million years ago. Hagfish and lampreys are living jawless members of this phylum.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this phylum of animals that have a notochord at some stage of life, including all vertebrates.

tossups.p: In humans, the jelly-like nucleus pulposus [“pul-POH-sus”] inside each spinal disc is a leftover of the flexible rod that defines this phylum. Lancelets keep that rod for their whole lives.
tossups.r: That rod, the notochord, is replaced by a backbone in most vertebrates. For 10 points, name this phylum that includes all vertebrates.

tossups.p: In human embryos, structures called pharyngeal pouches help form parts of the ear and throat, while a short tail shrinks away to leave the tailbone, or coccyx [“KOK-siks”]. Those features show that humans belong to this phylum.
tossups.r: In fish, the matching slits become gills. For 10 points, name this phylum defined by a notochord and a dorsal hollow nerve cord.

tossups.p: Sea squirts, also called ascidians [“uh-SID-ee-unz”], start life as swimming, tadpole-like larvae in this phylum before gluing themselves to rocks. Members of this phylum and echinoderms are deuterostomes, whose embryos form the anus before the mouth.
tossups.r: This phylum’s name comes from a Latin word meaning “cord.” For 10 points, name this phylum of animals with a notochord.

tossups.p: A 2006 DNA study concluded that tunicates, not lancelets, are the closest living relatives of vertebrates. Hagfish and lampreys are jawless members of this phylum, and lamprey larvae filter-feed in riverbed mud much like lancelets do.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this phylum whose members, including sharks and humans, have a notochord at some stage.

tossups.p: Barrel-shaped salps in this phylum can link up into long chains and swim by squirting water out of their bodies. Like other tunicates, salps build their tough outer covering with cellulose.
tossups.r: This phylum also includes lancelets and vertebrates. For 10 points, name this phylum defined by a notochord, a dorsal hollow nerve cord, and pharyngeal slits.

tossups.p: The tube-shaped heart of a tunicate in this phylum regularly reverses the direction in which it pumps blood. Some sea squirts also pack their blood cells with unusually large amounts of the metal vanadium.
tossups.r: In vertebrates, this phylum’s dorsal hollow nerve cord becomes the spinal cord. For 10 points, name this phylum that includes all vertebrates.

tossups.p: When the tadpole-like larva of a sea squirt settles on a rock, it absorbs its own tail and loses most of the hallmark traits of this phylum. Lancelets, by contrast, keep all of those traits for life.
tossups.r: Those traits include a notochord and pharyngeal slits. For 10 points, name this animal phylum that includes fish, birds, and humans.

clues.t: The phylum that includes all vertebrates: fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds, and mammals, including humans
Every member has a notochord, a flexible rod along the back, at some stage of life
Hallmark traits: notochord, dorsal hollow nerve cord, pharyngeal slits, and a post-anal tail
In most vertebrates, a backbone replaces the notochord
Three subphyla: vertebrates, tunicates (sea squirts), and lancelets
Sea squirt larvae look like tadpoles and show all four traits, but the adults lose most of them
Lancelets (amphioxus) are small fishlike filter feeders that burrow in sand and keep all four traits as adults
The dorsal hollow nerve cord becomes the brain and spinal cord in vertebrates
Pharyngeal slits become gills in fish; in human embryos, the matching pouches help form parts of the ear and throat
Deuterostomes, like echinoderms: the embryo’s first opening becomes the anus, not the mouth
Human embryos have a tail that shrinks away, leaving the tailbone, or coccyx
The name comes from a Latin word meaning “cord” or “string”
Hagfish and lampreys are its living jawless members
Pikaia, from the Burgess Shale, described by Charles Walcott in 1911, was long considered one of its earliest members
Haikouichthys, from China’s Chengjiang fossils, is one of its earliest known fishlike members, over 500 million years old
Walter Garstang (1928) proposed that vertebrates evolved from tadpole-like sea squirt larvae that never took the adult form
A 2006 DNA study found tunicates, not lancelets, to be the closest living relatives of vertebrates
Tunicates stiffen their tough outer tunic with cellulose, which no other animals are known to make
The endostyle, a food-trapping groove in tunicates, lancelets, and larval lampreys (ammocoetes), matches the vertebrate thyroid gland
Larvaceans are tunicates that keep their tadpole shape for life and build mucus “houses” to filter food
Salps are barrel-shaped tunicates that link into chains and swim by jet propulsion
Segmented muscle blocks called myomeres, V-shaped in lancelets, flex the bodies of lancelets and fish
In humans, the notochord’s leftover is the jelly-like nucleus pulposus inside each spinal disc
Acorn worms have pharyngeal slits but belong to a separate phylum, related to the echinoderms
Tunicate hearts regularly reverse the direction they pump; some sea squirts store the metal vanadium in their blood cells
When a sea squirt larva settles on a rock, it absorbs its own tail and loses most hallmark traits

trap.title: Phylum or subphylum?
trap.body: Vertebrates are only one subphylum of this phylum, alongside tunicates and lancelets, so answering “vertebrates” for a question about the whole phylum is wrong. Acorn worms (hemichordates) and echinoderms are close relatives in other phyla, and “deuterostomes” is a bigger group that only earns a prompt.
trap.fix: If the clues mention tunicates, sea squirts, lancelets, or traits found “at some stage of life,” answer chordates. If the clues are all about a backbone and the question says “this subphylum,” answer vertebrates. Acorn worms on their own mean hemichordates.
trap.line: Real answer line: Chordates (accept Chordata; do not accept “vertebrates”)

topics.name: Coral reefs
topics.kicker: Ocean structures built by coral polyps · The “rainforests of the sea”
topics.dates: Found in warm, shallow tropical seas
topics.briefing: Coral reefs look like rocky gardens, but they are built by animals: tiny coral polyps, cousins of jellyfish, that stack up limestone skeletons over thousands of years. Algae living inside the polyps feed them and give them color, so reefs grow best in warm, shallow, sunny water. Reefs cover less than 1 percent of the ocean floor, yet about a quarter of all ocean species live on or around them.
topics.answerHtml: Coral reefs (accept coral reef ecosystems; prompt on reefs or corals; do not accept “atolls” or “Great Barrier Reef”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Drilling at Enewetak [“EN-ih-WEE-tok”] Atoll in 1952 hit volcanic rock more than a kilometer down, confirming Charles Darwin’s idea that ring-shaped versions of these structures grow upward around slowly sinking volcanic islands.
tossups.r: Tiny polyps build these structures out of calcium carbonate. For 10 points, name these ocean ecosystems, the largest of which is the Great Barrier Reef.

tossups.p: Charles Darwin studied ring-shaped examples of these structures at the Cocos, or Keeling, Islands in 1836 during the voyage of the _Beagle_. His 1842 book sorted these structures into fringing, barrier, and atoll types.
tossups.r: These structures are built by colonies of coral polyps. For 10 points, name these underwater ecosystems found in warm, shallow tropical seas.

tossups.p: Many of the animals that build these structures release their eggs and sperm all at once on a few nights after a full moon, a mass spawning that clouds the water like an underwater snowstorm. The timing is set partly by water temperature and moonlight.
tossups.r: Those animals are coral polyps, which get most of their food from algae living in their tissues. For 10 points, name these underwater structures, such as the Great Barrier Reef.

tossups.p: Red algae that lay down their own limestone help cement these structures together. Parrotfish bite off and grind up chunks of these structures, turning them into much of the white sand on nearby beaches.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these underwater structures built by tiny coral polyps, nicknamed the “rainforests of the sea.”

tossups.p: A few animals that build these structures live in cold, dark water off Norway, but most depend on sunlight because they host dinoflagellates [“dy-noh-FLAJ-uh-lits”] called zooxanthellae [“zoh-uh-zan-THEL-ee”] inside their tissues. Without those partners, the builders slowly starve.
tossups.r: Hot water can make the builders expel those partners and turn white, a process called bleaching. For 10 points, name these tropical ocean structures built by coral polyps.

tossups.p: The Mesoamerican system of these structures, which runs along the coast of Belize, is the largest in the Western Hemisphere. Divers explore a giant underwater sinkhole called the Great Blue Hole inside it.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these ocean ecosystems, including the Great Barrier Reef, that are built by tiny animals called coral polyps.

tossups.p: Elkhorn and staghorn kinds of the animals that build these structures were listed as threatened in 2006, after disease wiped out most of them in the Caribbean. Their antler-shaped colonies grow in shallow water, where they help break up storm waves.
tossups.r: Ocean acidification makes it harder for those animals to build their calcium carbonate skeletons. For 10 points, name these underwater structures built by coral polyps.

tossups.p: Whale sharks gather each year at Ningaloo, a fringing example of these structures that lies close to the shore of Western Australia. Along the Florida Keys lies the only living barrier-type example of these structures in the continental United States.
tossups.r: In 1981, the largest of these structures, the Great Barrier Reef, became a UNESCO World Heritage Site. For 10 points, name these ecosystems built by coral polyps.

tossups.p: The tiny animals that build these structures often stretch out tentacles at night to catch plankton, stinging their prey with cells called nematocysts [“nih-MAT-uh-sists”]. Those builders are cnidarians, related to jellyfish and sea anemones.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these underwater structures, such as the Great Barrier Reef, built from calcium carbonate.

tossups.p: A region around Indonesia, the Philippines, and Papua New Guinea holds more kinds of the builders of these ecosystems than anywhere else. These ecosystems cover less than 1 percent of the ocean floor but shelter about a quarter of all ocean species.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these underwater ecosystems built by coral polyps and nicknamed the “rainforests of the sea.”

tossups.p: Crown-of-thorns starfish have destroyed large areas of these structures by climbing onto their builders and digesting them. Carbon dioxide dissolving in seawater also makes it harder for those builders to make their skeletons.
tossups.r: Clownfish in the film _Finding Nemo_ live in one of these structures. For 10 points, name these underwater ecosystems built by coral polyps.

tossups.p: Dinoflagellates long grouped in the genus Symbiodinium [“sim-bee-oh-DIN-ee-um”] live inside the animals that build these structures and give them most of their food and color, a partnership called mutualism. Those partners pass along sugars made by photosynthesis in exchange for shelter and nutrients.
tossups.r: Hot water can make the builders expel those partners and turn white. For 10 points, name these ocean structures, the largest of which lies off Australia.

tossups.p: Fringing examples of these structures grow right along a shore, while barrier examples are separated from land by a lagoon. A third type, the atoll, forms a ring around a lagoon after the island in the middle sinks away.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these underwater structures built by colonies of coral polyps in warm, shallow seas.

tossups.p: Each tiny animal that builds these structures pulls calcium and carbonate from seawater to make a cup-shaped limestone skeleton, and new ones grow on top of old ones. Many ancient layers of limestone rock began as these structures.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these ocean structures, such as the Great Barrier Reef, that grow in warm, shallow, sunlit water.

tossups.p: Sea fans, sea whips, and brain-shaped colonies grow on these structures, which also shelter sea turtles, moray eels, and giant clams. Those giant clams, like the builders of these structures, keep algae in their tissues.
tossups.r: Polyps build these structures in warm, shallow, sunlit water. For 10 points, name these ecosystems, the largest of which is the Great Barrier Reef.

clues.t: Built by colonies of tiny coral polyps that make hard calcium carbonate (limestone) skeletons
The largest is the Great Barrier Reef off Queensland, Australia
Nicknamed the “rainforests of the sea” for their huge variety of life
Grow best in warm, shallow, clear, sunlit tropical seas
Threatened by bleaching: stressed by hot water, the polyps expel their algae and turn white
The polyps get most of their food and color from algae called zooxanthellae living in their tissues, a mutualism
Three main types: fringing (along the shore), barrier (behind a lagoon), and ring-shaped atolls
Charles Darwin’s 1842 book explained that atolls form as they grow upward around slowly sinking volcanic islands
The builders are cnidarians, related to jellyfish and sea anemones, and sting prey with cells called nematocysts
Ocean acidification from dissolved carbon dioxide makes it harder for polyps to build skeletons
The crown-of-thorns starfish eats the polyps and has destroyed large areas of them
Cover less than 1 percent of the ocean floor but shelter about a quarter of all ocean species
Parrotfish grind up their hard parts and turn them into much of the white sand on nearby beaches
Clownfish shelter in sea anemones there; _Finding Nemo_ is set partly on the Great Barrier Reef
Drilling at Enewetak Atoll in 1952 hit volcanic rock more than a kilometer down, confirming Darwin’s idea
Darwin studied atolls at the Cocos (Keeling) Islands in 1836 during the voyage of the _Beagle_
Many polyps release eggs and sperm all at once on a few nights after a full moon, a mass spawning
Red coralline algae, which make their own limestone, help cement them together
A few reef-building corals live in cold, dark water, as off Norway, without algae partners
The Coral Triangle, around Indonesia, the Philippines, and Papua New Guinea, holds the most kinds of corals
The Mesoamerican Barrier Reef along Belize is the largest in the Western Hemisphere; the Great Blue Hole lies inside it
The Florida Keys hold the only living coral barrier reef in the continental U.S.; Ningaloo in Western Australia draws whale sharks
The Great Barrier Reef, about 2,300 kilometers long, became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1981
Elkhorn and staghorn corals, key Caribbean builders, were listed as threatened in 2006 after disease killed most of them
Their algae partners are dinoflagellates, long grouped in the genus Symbiodinium
Polyps often stretch out their tentacles at night to catch plankton
Each polyp builds a cup-shaped limestone skeleton on top of older ones; many ancient limestone layers began this way

trap.title: Reef, coral, or atoll?
trap.body: Saying just “coral” names the animals, not the structure they build, and “reef” alone is too general; both earn only a prompt. An atoll is one ring-shaped kind of coral reef, and the Great Barrier Reef is one famous example, so neither is the general answer.
trap.fix: When the question says “these structures” or “these ecosystems,” answer “coral reefs.” Answer “corals” only if it asks for “these animals” or “these cnidarians,” and “atolls” only if it asks for the ring-shaped islands that circle a lagoon.
trap.line: Real answer line: Coral reefs (prompt on reefs or corals; do not accept “atolls”)

topics.name: Dopamine
topics.kicker: Chemical messenger in the brain · Key to movement, motivation, and reward
topics.dates: First made in a lab in 1910
topics.briefing: Dopamine is a chemical messenger that nerve cells use to signal each other, and it helps your brain control movement and decide what is worth working for. Brain cells build it from the amino acid tyrosine, mostly in two small midbrain regions, including a dark patch called the substantia nigra. Losing many of the dopamine-making cells there causes Parkinson’s disease, which brings shaking and slow, stiff movements.
topics.answerHtml: Dopamine (prompt on neurotransmitter or catecholamine; do not accept “L-DOPA,” “serotonin,” or “norepinephrine”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Arvid Carlsson gave L-DOPA to rabbits that had been left unable to move by the drug reserpine, and they moved again because their brains turned it into this chemical. Carlsson shared the 2000 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for showing that this chemical is a neurotransmitter.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this brain chemical linked to movement and reward, whose shortage causes Parkinson’s disease.

tossups.p: In 1960, Oleh Hornykiewicz [“hor-nee-KEH-vitch”] found that brain tissue from people with a certain movement disorder held far less of this chemical than normal. That finding led doctors to treat the disorder with L-DOPA, which the brain turns into this chemical.
tossups.r: That disorder is Parkinson’s disease. For 10 points, name this neurotransmitter linked to the brain’s reward system.

tossups.p: George Barger and James Ewens first made this compound in a London lab in 1910, decades before anyone knew that the brain uses it. Cells in the body make this compound from the amino acid tyrosine.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this neurotransmitter tied to movement, motivation, and reward, whose loss causes Parkinson’s disease.

tossups.p: Oliver Sacks’s book _Awakenings_ describes patients left frozen for decades by an illness called encephalitis lethargica [“en-sef-uh-LY-tis luh-THAR-jih-kuh”] who briefly “woke up” in 1969 after taking a drug that the brain turns into this chemical. Robin Williams played a doctor based on Sacks in the 1990 film version.
tossups.r: That drug was L-DOPA. For 10 points, name this neurotransmitter whose loss in the brain causes Parkinson’s disease.

tossups.p: Wolfram Schultz found that monkey brain cells that release this chemical fire strongly when a reward comes as a surprise, but dip below their usual rate when an expected reward fails to arrive, a signal called a reward prediction error.
tossups.r: This chemical is made in the midbrain’s substantia nigra. For 10 points, name this neurotransmitter linked to motivation and reward.

tossups.p: In 1954, James Olds and Peter Milner found that rats would press a lever over and over to send small electric pulses into certain parts of their brains. Later research tied that behavior to brain circuits that use this chemical.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this neurotransmitter, often called a “feel-good” chemical, whose loss causes Parkinson’s disease.

tossups.p: As cells in the substantia nigra [“sub-STAN-shuh NY-gruh”] make this chemical, some of it turns into a dark pigment called neuromelanin, which gives that brain region its name, meaning “black substance.”
tossups.r: Losing those cells causes Parkinson’s disease. For 10 points, name this neurotransmitter that helps control movement and is linked to reward.

tossups.p: This molecule, with the formula C8H11NO2, has a benzene ring carrying two hydroxyl groups, called a catechol [“KAT-uh-kol”], linked to an amine group. Enzymes called MAO and COMT break this molecule down after it is released.
tossups.r: This chemical is made from the amino acid tyrosine. For 10 points, name this neurotransmitter, a catecholamine linked to reward and movement.

tossups.p: Cells in the hypothalamus release this chemical to stop the pituitary gland from making prolactin, a hormone that triggers milk production. That signal travels along the tuberoinfundibular [“too-buh-roh-in-fun-DIB-yuh-lur”] pathway, one of four major pathways that carry this chemical.
tossups.r: In the midbrain, the substantia nigra makes this chemical to help control movement. For 10 points, name this neurotransmitter whose loss causes Parkinson’s disease.

tossups.p: The enzyme tyrosine hydroxylase carries out the slowest step in making this chemical, turning the amino acid tyrosine into L-DOPA. Another enzyme then turns L-DOPA into this chemical, which cells can later convert into norepinephrine.
tossups.r: Losing the cells that make it causes Parkinson’s disease. For 10 points, name this neurotransmitter, often linked to pleasure and reward.

tossups.p: This chemical acts on five kinds of receptors, named D1 through D5, which fall into two families. After it signals, a transporter protein pulls it back into the nerve cell that released it, a process called reuptake.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this neurotransmitter, made from tyrosine, that is central to the brain’s reward system.

tossups.p: The nigrostriatal [“ny-groh-stry-AY-tul”] pathway carries this chemical from the substantia nigra to the striatum, part of the basal ganglia that helps start and smooth out movements. The cells that send it also make a dark pigment called neuromelanin.
tossups.r: Damage to that pathway causes the tremors and slow movements of Parkinson’s disease. For 10 points, name this neurotransmitter made from tyrosine.

tossups.p: The mesolimbic pathway carries this chemical from the ventral tegmental [“teg-MEN-tul”] area to the nucleus accumbens [“uh-KUM-benz”], deep in the forebrain. Cells in the ventral tegmental area also send this chemical to the prefrontal cortex along a separate pathway.
tossups.r: Rewards, especially surprising ones, cause bursts of this chemical. For 10 points, name this neurotransmitter, often called a “feel-good” chemical.

tossups.p: Doctors cannot treat a shortage of this chemical simply by giving it to patients, because it cannot cross the blood-brain barrier, so they give its precursor, L-DOPA, instead. That precursor was first tested as a treatment for that shortage in 1961.
tossups.r: That shortage causes Parkinson’s disease, which brings tremors and slow movement. For 10 points, name this neurotransmitter linked to movement and reward.

tossups.p: Nerve cells and adrenal gland cells turn this catecholamine into norepinephrine, and adrenal cells can then turn norepinephrine into epinephrine. In the brain, this chemical is made mainly in the substantia nigra and the ventral tegmental area.
tossups.r: Losing the cells that make this chemical causes Parkinson’s disease. For 10 points, name this neurotransmitter tied to motivation, pleasure, and reward.

clues.t: A neurotransmitter: a chemical messenger that carries signals between nerve cells
Central to the brain’s reward system, motivation, and pleasure
Helps control movement; losing the brain cells that make it causes Parkinson’s disease
Often called a “feel-good” chemical, along with serotonin and endorphins
Built from the amino acid tyrosine, by way of L-DOPA
A catecholamine; cells turn it into norepinephrine, which can become epinephrine
In the brain, made mainly in the substantia nigra (“black substance”) and the ventral tegmental area of the midbrain
Parkinson’s is treated with L-DOPA (levodopa), which crosses the blood-brain barrier and turns into it
Arvid Carlsson showed in the 1950s that it is a neurotransmitter and shared the 2000 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine
Oliver Sacks’s _Awakenings_ tells of patients who briefly “woke up” on L-DOPA in 1969; Robin Williams starred in the 1990 film
After signaling, a transporter protein pulls it back into the sending cell, a process called reuptake
First made in a London lab in 1910 by George Barger and James Ewens
Oleh Hornykiewicz found in 1960 that brains affected by Parkinson’s held far less of it, which led to L-DOPA treatment
Carlsson got rabbits left unable to move by the drug reserpine moving again by giving them L-DOPA
Wolfram Schultz showed that its cells in monkeys fire for surprise rewards and dip when expected rewards fail to come: a “reward prediction error”
James Olds and Peter Milner (1954) found rats would press a lever again and again to stimulate reward areas of their brains
The mesolimbic reward pathway carries it from the ventral tegmental area to the nucleus accumbens; a separate pathway carries it to the prefrontal cortex
The nigrostriatal pathway carries it from the substantia nigra to the striatum, part of the basal ganglia
Some of it turns into neuromelanin, the dark pigment that gives the substantia nigra its color
A catechol (benzene ring with two hydroxyl groups) linked to an amine; formula C8H11NO2; broken down by MAO and COMT
Released by the hypothalamus along the tuberoinfundibular pathway, it stops the pituitary from making the hormone prolactin
Acts on five receptor types, D1 through D5, which fall into two families
The enzyme tyrosine hydroxylase makes L-DOPA, the slowest step in building it
It cannot cross the blood-brain barrier itself, so doctors give its precursor instead

trap.title: Which feel-good chemical?
trap.body: Dopamine, serotonin, endorphins, and oxytocin are all called “feel-good” or “happy” chemicals in pop culture, so a quick buzz can grab the wrong one. L-DOPA is the building block that becomes dopamine, not dopamine itself, and norepinephrine and epinephrine are made from dopamine, so all three are wrong here.
trap.fix: Parkinson’s disease, the substantia nigra, L-DOPA, tyrosine, reward, and motivation point to dopamine. Mood, sleep, the gut, and the amino acid tryptophan point to serotonin. The fight-or-flight response points to epinephrine.
trap.line: Real answer line: Dopamine (do not accept “L-DOPA” or “serotonin”)

topics.name: Food chains
topics.kicker: Who eats whom in nature · Shows how energy flows from producers to predators
topics.briefing: A food chain shows who eats whom: grass is eaten by a grasshopper, which is eaten by a frog, which is eaten by a snake, which is eaten by a hawk. Each link passes along only about a tenth of its energy, because most is used up or lost as heat, so food chains rarely have more than four or five links. Tangle many food chains together and you get a food web.
topics.answerHtml: Food chains (accept food chain; prompt on food webs; do not accept “trophic levels” or “energy pyramid”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Charles Elton described these sequences, along with pyramids of numbers, in his 1927 book _Animal Ecology_. He noted that the large animals near the end of these sequences are usually much rarer than the small ones near the start.
tossups.r: Each one starts with a producer, such as a plant, and arrows show which organism eats which. For 10 points, name these diagrams of feeding relationships.

tossups.p: The 9th-century Arab writer al-Jahiz [“al-JAH-hiz”] described animals eating one another in an early version of these sequences in his _Book of Animals_. Each step in one of these sequences is called a trophic [“TROH-fik”] level.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these sequences that show who eats whom, starting with producers like plants and algae.

tossups.p: Raymond Lindeman’s 1942 study of Cedar Bog Lake in Minnesota measured how energy passes along these sequences, and it helped lead to the rule that only about 10 percent of the energy at one step reaches the next.
tossups.r: Arrows in these sequences point from the eaten to the eater. For 10 points, name these diagrams that show how energy moves from producers to consumers.

tossups.p: Rachel Carson’s _Silent Spring_ warned that the pesticide DDT becomes more concentrated at each step up these sequences, a process called biomagnification. That buildup thinned the eggshells of bald eagles and brown pelicans.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these sequences of who eats whom, which start with producers and end with top predators.

tossups.p: At deep-sea hydrothermal vents discovered in 1977, these sequences begin not with plants but with bacteria that make food from hydrogen sulfide through chemosynthesis. Giant tube worms at those vents carry such bacteria inside their bodies.
tossups.r: On land, these sequences usually begin with plants. For 10 points, name these diagrams that show which organisms eat which.

tossups.p: Sea otters eat sea urchins, which eat kelp, so when otters disappear, urchins can destroy whole kelp forests. That ripple effect from the top of one of these sequences down to its base is called a trophic cascade.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these sequences that show the order in which living things eat one another, from producers to top predators.

tossups.p: Robert Paine removed Pisaster [“pih-SAS-ter”] starfish from tide pools in Washington State and watched mussels crowd out other species, leading him to coin the term “keystone species.” Paine also named the trophic cascade, an effect that travels down these sequences.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these diagrams of feeding relationships, in which energy flows from producers to consumers.

tossups.p: After wolves returned to Yellowstone National Park in 1995, scientists studied whether fear of them changed where elk grazed, a possible trophic cascade down one of these sequences. Wolves are apex predators, with no natural predators of their own.
tossups.r: Plants form the first link of most of these sequences. For 10 points, name these diagrams that show who eats whom.

tossups.p: Detritus-based versions of these sequences begin with dead plant and animal matter eaten by detritivores [“dih-TRY-tuh-vorz”] such as earthworms, unlike grazing versions that begin with living plants. In many forests, more energy flows through the detritus-based versions than through the grazing ones.
tossups.r: Decomposers such as bacteria and fungi recycle nutrients at every step. For 10 points, name these sequences showing how energy passes from organism to organism.

tossups.p: In the open ocean, a pyramid of biomass can be upside down, since fast-growing phytoplankton are eaten almost as quickly as they grow. Ocean versions of these sequences often run from phytoplankton to krill to fish to seals.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these diagrams that show which organisms eat which, starting with producers.

tossups.p: Net primary productivity measures the energy that the first organisms in these sequences store after using some for their own respiration. Because the second law of thermodynamics means energy is lost as heat at each step, these sequences rarely have more than four or five links.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these sequences that start with producers and show who eats whom.

tossups.p: A pyramid of numbers, sometimes called an Eltonian pyramid, counts the organisms at each step of these sequences. In _The Lion King_, Mufasa describes one of these sequences that loops back on itself: lions eat antelope, but when lions die, their bodies become the grass that antelope eat.
tossups.r: Each one begins with a producer. For 10 points, name these sequences of feeding relationships that run from producers to consumers.

tossups.p: Mercury reaches high levels in big predatory fish such as swordfish and sharks, because those fish feed near the top of these sequences. Orcas, which have no natural predators, are apex predators at the top of ocean versions of these sequences.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these sequences that show who eats whom, beginning with producers such as algae.

tossups.p: Each step of these sequences is a trophic level, from a Greek word for “nourishment,” and only about a tenth of the energy at one step passes to the next. Most of the rest is lost as heat during cellular respiration.
tossups.r: Plants and algae are producers in these sequences, and herbivores are primary consumers. For 10 points, name these diagrams of who eats whom.

tossups.p: Because toxins build up at each step of these sequences, an osprey can carry far more of a pesticide than the fish it eats, and the fish far more than the plankton it eats. Ecologists call that buildup biomagnification.
tossups.r: Many of these sequences linked together form a food web. For 10 points, name these diagrams of who eats whom.

trap.title: Chain or web?
trap.body: A food chain is one straight line of who eats whom; a food web is many food chains woven together, so a question about one simple sequence wants “food chains” and one about a whole ecosystem’s network wants “food webs.” Trophic levels (the steps), energy pyramids, and trophic cascades are related ideas but different answers.
trap.fix: Listen to the noun and the shape. “This sequence” or “this series” means food chain. “This network” or “these interconnected” feeding links means food web. “These steps” or “these levels” means trophic levels, and a diagram that narrows as energy shrinks is an energy pyramid.
trap.line: Real answer line: Food chains (accept food chain; prompt on food webs; do not accept “trophic levels”)
